extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of Plato, classical literature, and literary/philosophical criticism
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Plato's evaluative standards (as discussed in the Republic, Book X and commentary) for judging poetry, drama, and other imitative arts, especially with respect to truth, moral effect, and civic usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry as imitation (thrice removed from truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet or painter is an imitator, and in the third degree removed from the truth (the painter imitates the carpenter's bed, which itself imitates the Form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's analogy: God makes the original, the craftsman makes the particular, the painter imitates the craftsman's product and thus is 'thrice removed.' The implication for evaluation is that poetic representations concern appearance not reality and so are epistemically inferior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry is devoid of knowledge; it is play or sport
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is devoid of knowledge, being only a kind of play or sport; the imitator has no true understanding of the things he depicts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contrast maker/user (who know the use and standard) with imitator (who can represent without understanding). Example: the flute-player knows good and bad flute, the maker trusts him, the imitator cannot judge. Use this to assess whether a poetic work conveys real knowledge or mere appearance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emotional effects: poetry injures by exciting the feelings
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry has the power of injuriously exciting the feelings; it feeds and waters the passions and lets them rule instead of being ruled by reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: lengthy lamentation encourages indulgence in sorrow; comedy's buffoonery can make audiences behave indecently at home. Evaluate poetry for whether it provokes unregulated sympathy or imitates vices rather than disciplining emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Usefulness as well as delight (educative function)
rubrics_metrics.description: If poetry cannot show that it is useful as well as delightful, it must be renounced—poetry must be useful like 'rational lovers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato's test: does the poet educate or improve the soul, or merely entertain? Works that are only pleasurable but not beneficial to moral or rational development should be excluded. This is the central criterion for permitting poetry in the ideal state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subordination to law and reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Not pleasure and pain, but law and reason shall rule in our State; poetry must not have authority over the mind of man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether a poem asserts moral authority or shapes belief in ways that circumvent reason or law. Allowed poetry must be compatible with civic norms and the rule of reason.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permitted content: hymns and praises; prohibited dramatic/imitative genres
rubrics_metrics.description: All poetry which goes beyond hymns to the Gods and praises of famous men is to be prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plato permits certain narrowly defined genres (religious praise, encomia) while excluding tragic and many dramatic/epic forms that mislead or corrupt. Evaluate by genre and thematic content against this permitted/prohibited distinction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical educational value (didactic efficacy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Poets are challenged to show any practical good they have done—laws given, modes of life instituted, or practical counsel for statesmanship.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete historical/functional tests: did the poet found a way of life, provide laws, or offer actionable arts? Homer is criticized for lacking such practical formative influence; this metric measures real-world educative impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Target of appeal: inferior (sensual) vs higher (intellectual) faculties
rubrics_metrics.description: The imitative arts are concerned with the inferior parts of the soul (passions, particulars of sense) while the higher faculties deal with universals and reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether a work primarily stimulates contingent sensual responses or whether it engages universal, rational understanding. Works that primarily address and empower lower faculties are judged negatively in Plato's framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Amenability to rule, measure, and calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic creations are not tested by rule and measure; they are only appearances, whereas calculation/measuring arts determine truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the art form can be subjected to rational criteria (rules, measures) that allow correct/incorrect judgments. Lack of such testability is a strike against reliability as a source of knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential to harmonize vs enervate the mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Arts might harmonize as well as enervate the mind; they can sometimes console and elevate, giving expression to deep or sad thoughts that otherwise cannot be expressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a mitigating/positive criterion: judge whether a given poetic work harmonizes, consoles, or elevates the audience (and thus might be permissible), rather than merely inflaming or weakening them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of role-playing on moral character (actor's integrity)
rubrics_metrics.description: The profession of an actor is a degradation: playing many parts tends to destroy the actor's own character; dramatic power is often inconsistent with firmness of mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic arts or performers, consider the potential for role-playing to erode personal moral integrity and whether dramatic skill correlates with weak character in practice (Plato's worry).

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's capacity to ennoble ordinary subjects by ideal expression
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist may ennoble ordinary objects (e.g., a bed) by imparting ideal interest in form and feeling; great works can embody the divine beyond mere imitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a countervailing criterion (modern/critic's reply): evaluate whether the poet/artist transcends mere imitation to express ideals or bring dignity/pathos to ordinary subjects—if so, the work gains positive aesthetic/moral value despite Plato's general objections.
